before: <para id="import-auto-id1870847">Medical doses of radiation are also limited. Diagnostic doses are generally low and have further lowered with improved techniques and faster films. With the possible exception of routine dental X-rays, radiation is used diagnostically only when needed so that the low risk is justified by the benefit of the diagnosis. Chest X-rays give the lowest doses—about 0.1 mSv to the tissue affected, with less than 5 percent scattering into tissues that are not directly imaged. Other X-ray procedures range upward to about 10 mSv in a CT scan, and about 5 mSv (0.5 rem) per dental X-ray, again both only affecting the tissue imaged. Medical images with radiopharmaceuticals give doses ranging from 1 to 5 mSv, usually localized. One exception is the thyroid scan using <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mrow/><m:mtext>131</m:mtext></m:msup><m:mtext>I</m:mtext></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"" lSup { size 8{"131"} } I} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>. Because of its relatively long half-life, it exposes the thyroid to about 0.75 Sv. The isotope <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mrow/><m:mtext>123</m:mtext></m:msup><m:mtext>I</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> is more difficult to produce, but its short half-life limits thyroid exposure to about 15 mSv.</para>
after: <para id="import-auto-id1870847">Medical doses of radiation are also limited. Diagnostic doses are generally low and have been further lowered with improved techniques and more efficient detectors. Radiation should be used diagnostically only when needed so that the risk is justified by the benefit of the diagnosis. Chest X-rays give low doses—about 0.1 mSv effective dose for an adult. Other X-ray procedures give higher doses, such as about 6 mSv in a chest CT scan. Dental X-ray doses depend on the type and number of images; a panoramic image of the whole mouth gives an effective dose of about 0.025 mSv. These are approximate values that vary with the patient and the technique used. Medical images with radiopharmaceuticals also involve radiation exposure. One example is the thyroid scan using <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mrow/><m:mtext>131</m:mtext></m:msup><m:mtext>I</m:mtext></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"" lSup { size 8{"131"} } I} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, which has a relatively long half-life of about 8 days and emits beta particles as well as gamma rays. The isotope <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mrow/><m:mtext>123</m:mtext></m:msup><m:mtext>I</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> has a shorter half-life of about 13 hours and does not emit beta-minus particles, which can reduce thyroid exposure in diagnostic imaging. The dose depends on the activity administered and how much of the isotope the thyroid takes up.</para>
